title: Copy & Clone

writing.exampleCaption: The integer copies; the `String` would have moved without `.clone()`.
writing.explanation:
Types whose fields are all `Copy` and which do not implement `Drop` can implement `Copy`, so assigning them leaves the original usable. An owning `String` or `Vec` is not `Copy`; duplicating those owners requires an explicit operation such as `.clone()` — the cost is visible in the source rather than hidden in an assignment.

`Copy` means a value can be duplicated by copying its bits, with no visible method call. Primitive integers and many small plain-data structs qualify. A type with a destructor cannot be `Copy`, because two implicit copies would both try to perform cleanup. `String` owns a heap allocation and therefore moves on ordinary assignment. `Clone` is different: it is an explicit operation, and its cost depends on the type. Cloning a `String` duplicates its bytes into a new buffer.

In the sample, `a` and `b` are separate integers after `let b = a`, so both print. The string expression uses `s.clone()` to create `t`; after that, both own their own text. If you change the line to `let t = s`, only `t` remains usable. The output may look identical when you do clone, but the memory and performance behavior are not. That is why Rust makes the expensive path visible.

Do not add `.clone()` automatically whenever the compiler reports a move. Ask whether the next operation only needs `&T`, whether ownership can be transferred to the right place, or whether two independent values are genuinely required. Try deriving `Copy` for a struct containing only `u32` fields, then add a `String` field and read the new error. This reveals the trait requirement through a concrete type. Use cloning when independent ownership is part of the design, and borrowing when the other code only needs temporary access.

An `Arc<T>` clone illustrates another nuance: it usually increments a reference count rather than duplicating all the data inside. The method name means an explicit duplicate of the value’s ownership handle, not necessarily a deep copy of every reachable byte.

`Copy` is a semantic contract, not a promise that the value is small or cheap: a large array of Copy elements is still Copy. `Clone` need not deep-copy data; cloning an `Arc<T>` shares the same allocation and increments its reference count. Decide whether the API needs another owner or independent data.
writing.feedback: Cloning creates a second owned `String`, so the original binding stays valid.
writing.question: How do you make that compile without changing the println?
writing.rule: `Copy` permits implicit bitwise duplication; `Clone` is explicit and has a type-specific cost.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: Copy duplicates implicitly; Clone duplicates only when you ask.
writing.task: Return two independent owned strings containing the borrowed input. The caller keeps its original text. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.

recall.question: What does `Arc::clone(&a)` duplicate, and what does it not?
recall.answer: It duplicates the handle and increments the reference count. It does not copy the vector, so this prints `2 true`: two owners pointing at the same allocation. `Clone` means another owner, not necessarily a deep copy.

recall.question: Why does this derive fail?
recall.answer: `Copy` needs every field to be `Copy`, and `String` owns a heap buffer that must be freed once, so implicit bitwise copies are not allowed (E0204). Drop `Copy` and keep `Clone`, so duplicating is an explicit `.clone()`.
